awd_titl_txt: Conference: Summer Program in Astrophysics 2025: Cool Frontiers: Exploring Dust and Ice in the Cosmos
awd_abstract_narration:
The University of Virginia will organize and host the 2025 Summer Program in Astrophysics (SPA), from June 23 to August 1, 2025.   The topic of the 2025 program will be “Cool Frontiers: Exploring Dust and Ice in the Cosmos.” The SPA is a unique graduate and postdoctoral training program which brings together world-class scientists with a wide breadth of technical skills and research interests, together with about fifteen graduate students to solve topical outstanding problems in astrophysics. The SPA operates in the summer for six weeks and has been hosted by various institutions world-wide over the past fourteen years.  

The program begins with a one-week workshop on a featured topic with morning introductory lectures by invited faculty and afternoon contributed presentations on state-of-the-art research by our long-term participants.  The remaining five weeks are devoted to student research, supplemented by daily seminars and discussions.  Astrophysical dust and ice play a critical role in the formation and evolution of planets, stars, and galaxies. Many questions about their properties, origin, and evolution remain. With access to forefront observational data, e.g., ALMA and JWST, which are providing unprecedented spatially and spectrally resolved views of dust and ice in different contexts, as well as theoretical models on all scales incorporating self-consistent, detailed treatments of the important physical and chemical processes, participants will work on projects that not only address fundamental and long-standing questions about dust and ice, but also ultimately have the potential to advance our understanding of stellar and planetary astrophysics, galaxy evolution and cosmology.  By design, the SPA trains a large number of graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, providing them with close mentoring by leading scientists in the field. The students acquire research skills during the program, while the postdocs gain mentoring and leadership skills.  The program is mindful of diversity, and has an excellent track record for training female scientists in particular.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The Kavli Summer Program in Astrophysics (KSPA) was hosted at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville from June 23 to August 1, 2025.  The theme, "Cool Frontiers: Exploring Dust and Ice in the Cosmos," focused on dust and ice, tiny solid particles that are essential ingredients in how stars and planets form, how galaxies evolve, and how we interpret what we observe with telescopes. 

Across cosmic history, dust absorbs energy released by stars and galaxies and re-emits it as infrared light, helping to create the cosmic infrared background. Dust also changes how galaxies look by absorbing and scattering starlight, producing interstellar polarization, and locking up certain heavy elements ("refractory" elements) from the interstellar gas. Dust is also central to star formation: it helps cool interstellar clouds so gravity can compress gas into new stars, and it can shield that gas from harsh ultraviolet radiation that would otherwise slow or prevent collapse. Ice, often in the form of icy mantles coating dust grains, plays a vital role in the chemistry of space by providing surfaces where complex organic molecules can form, including molecules relevant to the chemical pathways that precede life. In planet formation, dust and ice shape the structure and temperature of protoplanetary disks and act as the building blocks of planetesimals, which then merge to form planets. They also help deliver key materials such as silicates, hydrocarbons, and water, influencing the chemical diversity of planets and their atmospheres.

This award comes at a pivotal moment for the field. New observations, especially from the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), are providing unprecedented, detailed views of dust and ice in many settings, from the winds of cool giant stars and the debris of supernova explosions to planet-forming disks and even early galaxies. At the same time, theoretical models are becoming more realistic by including self-consistent physics and chemistry for how dust and ice form and evolve, including processes like nucleation and condensation, destruction and processing in shocks, and the effects of radiation. Together, these advances make it possible to tackle long-standing questions: How exactly do dust and ice form and get destroyed in different environments? How do grain sizes and compositions change as material cycles from dying stars into the interstellar medium and then into new stars and planets? How does dust shape galaxy evolution by regulating star formation and feedback? And how do the properties of dust and ice differ in extreme environments, from planetary atmospheres to the supermassive blackholes at the centers of galaxies?

The program's main intellectual outcome was to accelerate progress on these questions by pairing intensive training with hands-on, collaborative research. The first week provided a shared foundation through a series of in-depth, accessible lectures by leading experts, followed by research talks introducing active problems and methods in the field. After that, student fellows worked in small teams, each guided daily by faculty and postdoctoral mentors, to carry out focused research projects over five weeks. These projects spanned a wide range of topics, including dust and ice in planet-forming disks, dust production in stellar winds and supernovae, and dust processing in the interstellar medium and galactic environments. Students synthesized their results in final presentations and written research reports posted online (see https://kspa.soe.ucsc.edu/2025/students), with many projects in preparation or already submitted to peer-reviewed journals. 

The broader impacts were centered on training and community building. The program supported 13 graduate student fellows from a wide range of institutions in the U.S. and internationally, and engaged a large cohort of mentors and long-term participants, including many early-career scientists. In addition to 2 - 3 research seminars each week, the program included career panels and structured discussions on professional development, including career paths in and beyond academia, and practical guidance on the job-application process. The KSPA's immersive format provides close mentoring, strengthens technical and communication skills, and helps participants build lasting professional networks. Participant feedback indicated strong gains in collaboration opportunities and a significant positive influence on career trajectories. The program also strengthened institutional connections at the University of Virginia, including collaborations across Astronomy and Chemistry and with the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, and included educational visits (such as to the Green Bank Telescope and UVA's Nanoscale Materials Characterization Facility) that broadened participants' understanding of how major scientific facilities contribute to discovery. Overall, the award advanced knowledge in an active research frontier while developing the next generation of scientists equipped to work across disciplinary boundaries.
